idiom_name: Request& step(...) { ...; return *this; } - lvalue-reference chain with a terminal build()
implementation_notes: C++ writes the chain by hand: each step returns *this by reference (or a pointer), the terminal operation returns the product or performs the effect, and the standard library demonstrates exactly this shape - `std::ostream& operator<<` returns the stream so a whole output expression is one statement. Prefer *this by lvalue reference when a named builder is configured across conditionals or reused to spawn several products; add &&-qualified overloads returning std::move(*this) when temporaries are chained in a single expression, so the accumulated state is moved rather than copied. Because C++ has no polymorphic this before C++23's deducing this, a chain that must survive subclassing fixes its receiver with CRTP; otherwise every inherited step returns the base class and truncates the chain.
code_sketch:
Request req = Request::builder("https://api.example.com")
                  .method("POST")          // Request& method(const std::string&)
                  .timeout(std::chrono::seconds(10))
                  .build();                // terminal: validates, then moves the state
pitfalls: A step declared to return the builder by value copies the whole accumulated state at every link; return *this by reference (or std::move(*this) from an &&-qualified overload).
A chain that returns a reference into a temporary (`auto& b = Builder{}.host("h");`) dangles at the end of the full expression; bind the result by value or keep the builder in a named variable.
Inherited steps return the base type unless the return type is fixed (CRTP, or C++23 deducing this), so a subclass's chain silently loses its extra steps.

variants.name: Rvalue-qualified steps for single-expression chains
variants.implementation_notes: Overload each step with && so a temporary builder is consumed instead of copied: `Builder&& step(...) && { ...; return std::move(*this); }`, with a matching `build() &&` marked [[nodiscard]]. Providing both overloads lets a named builder use the lvalue form (reusable, configurable across conditionals) while `Builder{}.a().b().build()` moves the state through the chain with no copies; ref-qualified member functions are the C++11 feature that makes the split expressible, and they exist precisely because the two call styles have different ownership needs.
variants.code_sketch:
auto req = Request::builder()
                .method("POST")   // rvalue overload moves the state forward
                .timeout(10s)
                .build();        // [[nodiscard]] Request build() &&
pitfalls: Mixing conventions breaks chaining: &-qualified steps return an lvalue reference that cannot be consumed by `build() &&`, and &&-qualified steps cannot be called on a named builder at all - both overloads must be provided.
`std::move(*this)` inside a step that was called on an lvalue silently guts the named builder; guard it with the && qualifier so the compiler rejects the lvalue call.
